title: The floods that carved the Scablands
text: A dam of ice holds back a lake in Montana — then breaks, again and again, and the floods tear across Washington. 20,000 years ago the great ice sheet over western Canada pushes tongues of ice south into what is now the United States. One tongue of ice blocks the Clark Fork River in Idaho like a dam. Behind it, water fills the valleys of western Montana: Glacial Lake Missoula. Ice floats on water. When the lake grows deep enough, the water lifts the dam and breaks it. The lake empties within days. A wall of water rushes across eastern Washington, stripping off the soil and cutting deep channels into the rock: the Channeled Scablands. The water backs up behind narrow gaps in the hills, then roars down the Columbia River gorge, past where Portland is today, and out to the Pacific. The ice pushes forward again, the dam forms again, and the lake fills again. It happens over and over — dozens of times. About 15,000 years ago the ice melts back for good, and the floods stop. In 1923 the geologist J Harlen Bretz said that a giant flood had made the Scablands. Other geologists scoffed. Decades later, he was proved right.
prompt:
A painting for a natural-history museum: The floods that carved the Scablands, about 20,000 years ago.
Painted in the manner of Charles R. Knight (1874–1953), the American natural-history muralist: oil on canvas, confident visible brushwork, warm golden naturalistic light, soft atmospheric haze, a palette of ochres, siennas, olive greens and dusty blues, calm and dignified realism. Keep his warmth and his eye for the real world, but follow TODAY's science, not the science of his time: paint the land, water, plants and climate exactly as described here.
What happened, from the scientific evidence: A dam of ice holds back a lake in Montana — then breaks, again and again, and the floods tear across Washington. 20,000 years ago the great ice sheet over western Canada pushes tongues of ice south into what is now the United States. One tongue of ice blocks the Clark Fork River in Idaho like a dam. Behind it, water fills the valleys of western Montana: Glacial Lake Missoula. Ice floats on water. When the lake grows deep enough, the water lifts the dam and breaks it. The lake empties within days. A wall of water rushes across eastern Washington, stripping off the soil and cutting deep channels into the rock: the Channeled Scablands. The water backs up behind narrow gaps in the hills, then roars down the Columbia River gorge, past where Portland is today, and out to the Pacific. The ice pushes forward again, the dam forms again, and the lake fills again. It happens over and over — dozens of times. About 15,000 years ago the ice melts back for good, and the floods stop. In 1923 the geologist J Harlen Bretz said that a giant flood had made the Scablands. Other geologists scoffed. Decades later, he was proved right.
Paint the moment as seen from high in the sky: a wide view of the land and sea where it happened, as they were THEN — the continents, coasts, plants and life of that time, not today's. Show only what the description says. Living things only where it names them, small, as they are reconstructed today; none where it does not.
No text, labels, map lines, arrows, borders or frame.
differs: The floods are shown all at once; they came again and again over thousands of years.
